## Question 1 (Translating a Result)

A randomized trial of a brief sleep-hygiene intervention reports the following:

> Participants assigned to the intervention reported lower insomnia severity at follow-up than those assigned to the waitlist, *b* = --2.4, 95% CI [--4.1, --0.7], *t*(118) = 2.80, *p* = .006, *d* = 0.51.

a) Translate this result into two or three sentences for a general audience — say, a newspaper reader — without using the words "significant," "*p*-value," or "confidence interval."

b) Explain which part of the original result was hardest to express in plain language, and how you handled it.{{< hp glyph="i" >}}

## Question 2 (Spotting Overstatement)

Below are four attempts to translate that same sleep-hygiene result (*b* = --2.4, 95% CI [--4.1, --0.7], *p* = .006, *d* = 0.51) for a general audience. For each one, state whether it is an acceptable translation, and if it is not, name specifically what it gets wrong.{{< hp glyph="i" >}}

i. "The intervention reduced insomnia severity by about 2.4 points on average, though the true benefit could plausibly be as small as 0.7 points or as large as 4.1."

ii. "There is a 99.4% chance that the intervention works."

iii. "The intervention cured insomnia in half of the participants."

iv. "The study found no evidence that the intervention failed to help."

## Question 3 (Translating Your Own Work)

a) Take a statistical result from your own research (or, if you do not have one yet, from any paper in your area) and write two versions of it: one as it would appear in a results section, and one as you would explain it to a participant in the study who asked what you found.

b) Compare your two versions. What information was lost in the plain-language version, and was any of it information the listener actually needed?{{< hp glyph="i" >}}
